docs.text: The language ¶ This page describes Rhema as the compiler implements it, construct by construct. The tutorial introduces the same material in order of use; the grammar at the end summarises the syntax. Files ¶ A Rhema file is a sequence of declarations , in any order, encoded as UTF-8 and named with the extension .rhm . A file does one or more of three things: declares questions : a start symbol, a prompt and an answer, at the top level (the question main ) or in question blocks; declares sets : whole assignments built from questions; provides productions and attributes for other files to include or import . A file with neither questions nor sets is a library : it can be checked, included and imported, but not run. polynomial_core.rhm and matrix_core.rhm in the standard library are libraries. Lexical structure ¶ Comments run from # to the end of the line. Identifiers are a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores. By convention nonterminals start with a capital letter ( E , Q ) and attributes, randoms and lets do not; the language does not require it. Integers are decimal digits. A minus sign is an operator, except where a declaration takes a signed integer: the value in attribute , starting values in question blocks, and the draws of a set . Strings are written in double quotes and may span lines; the line breaks are part of the string. The only escapes are \" (a quote) and \\ (a backslash). Any other backslash is kept, so LaTeX is written directly: "\cdot" and "\\cdot" are the same string. Keywords are reserved: answer as attribute boolean context copy import include left let mistake nonassoc on precedence prompt question random require right set split start synth weight when width and or not true false A reserved word cannot be used as a name, also not for a local name in a production: let width = ... is a syntax error. Inside a set block, the words part , of , any , in , spread , low , allowed , distinct , balanced and ordered have a meaning, but they are not reserved and may be used as names elsewhere. Attributes ¶ Inherited attributes ¶ attribute NAME = INTEGER [ copy | split ] declares an attribute whose value travels down the tree. INTEGER is its value at the root of a question, and must not be negative. The distribution says how a node passes it to its children: copy (the default) every child that is a symbol of the grammar receives the node's value; split the node's value is divided between those children, every division into non-negative whole numbers being equally likely. Leaves (generators and quoted words) receive nothing. A child that is a module symbol ( alias.F ) counts as a symbol of the grammar. The starting value can be changed from outside, with --set NAME=VALUE on the command line, an INTEGER in a question block, or a draw in a set . Synthesized attributes ¶ synth NAME synth NAME on SYMBOL declares an attribute whose value travels up the tree, computed at a node from its children. on SYMBOL restricts it to one nonterminal; without it, every nonterminal must compute it. The same name may be declared on several symbols, but not both with and without on . Every production for a symbol must compute every synthesized attribute that symbol carries. A generator leaf carries one attribute, value , the number it drew; a quoted word carries value , its text. Three names are reserved for the start symbol: pg_context , the WeBWorK context of each question, pg_width , the width of its answer blanks, and pg_variables , the variables of its formula and proposition answers. When the start symbol computes the first two, they override the file's context and width for that question. pg_variables is text naming variables, such as "x y" . A formula answer is written with a context that declares the variables it holds; with pg_variables every formula answer of the question is declared in all the named ones, so a derivative that comes to 6y is entered in a blank that knows x too. A proposition answer is declared in them in the same way, as propositional variables. It may also be a let of the file, for all its questions. Productions ¶ LHS -> SYMBOL ... [ when EXPR ] [ weight INTEGER ] { EQUATION ... } A production says that the nonterminal LHS may be made of the symbols on the right. The braces are required, even when empty. Each symbol on the right is one of: Written Meaning E a nonterminal, if the file has productions for it; otherwise a terminal that stands for its name + - * / % ^ a terminal that stands for the operator "text" a terminal that stands for the text integer_between(1, 9) a generator: a leaf that draws a number (see builtins ) calc.F or calc.F(cost = cost - 1) a nonterminal of an imported module, with starting values for its inherited attributes $1 , $2 , ... refer to these symbols, counting from 1. when EXPR is the production's guard . The production may be chosen only when it is true. It is evaluated before the children exist, so it may use inherited attributes and question-level values, but not $n . weight INTEGER (a positive integer, 1 by default) is the production's relative chance of being chosen among those whose guards hold. Equations ¶ The body holds equations and requirements, separated by line breaks or commas: NAME = EXPR , where NAME is inherited An update , applied before the children are built: the value is added to the attribute. It must not make the budget negative, and a positive constant is refused, because an update spends a budget. cost = -2 spends 2. NAME = EXPR , where NAME is synthesized Computes the attribute, after the children are built. An equation may use an attribute computed earlier in the same body by its bare name. require EXPR A condition checked after the children are built and the equations above it are computed. When it is false, the node is built again. let NAME = EXPR A local name : a value computed after the children are built, for the lines below it in the same body. The node does not carry it, so it needs no synth declaration and no other production sees it. The name must be new: an attribute, a random, a file-level let or an earlier local name of the same production is refused. Guards, updates and generator arguments are evaluated before the children exist and cannot use it. mistake NAME ATTRIBUTE = EXPR A mistake line : what a student who makes the mistake NAME computes for ATTRIBUTE here. It is skipped when the question is generated. Updates are applied in the order written; equations, local names and requirements are evaluated in the order written. B -> integer_between ( - 3 , 2 ) integer_between ( 1 , 4 ) { let upper = $1 . value + $2 . value require upper != 0 latex = "\int_ {" ++ str($1.value) ++ "} ^ {" ++ str(upper) ++ "} " value = upper } Expressions ¶ Form Meaning 12 , "text" a number, a string true , false the two truth values NAME an inherited attribute of the node, a random or let, or an attribute or local name computed earlier in the same production $2.NAME an attribute of the second child $2 the second child itself; only as an argument of infix and prefix S.NAME an attribute of the start symbol S ; only in prompt and answer alias.NAME a random or let of an imported module f(e, ...) a builtin function -e , not e negation e + e , - , * , / , % , ^ arithmetic on numbers e ++ e joining text, or text and answer blanks e = e , != , < , <= , > , >= comparison e and e , e or e logic Numbers are exact rationals: 1 / 3 is one third, not 0.333. = and != on text compare the strings, and on truth values they are the biconditional and exclusive or; < , <= , > and >= order numbers only. Operators bind, from loosest to tightest: or ; and ; not ; the comparisons (which do not chain); ++ (right-associative); + - ; * / % ; ^ (right-associative); unary - . Brackets group. Every value has a type, and rhema check finds the uses no type allows before anything is generated; see Types . Question-level values ¶ random NAME = boolean random NAME = GENERATOR ( INTEGER , ...) let NAME = EXPR A random is drawn once per question, before the tree is built, and has the same value wherever it is used. Its arguments must be integer literals. A let is computed once per question, after the randoms, from randoms and earlier lets. It may call any builtin function but may not refer to the tree. Types ¶ Every value has one of these types. Nothing in a file declares a type: the checker works them out. Type Made by number a literal, a generator, a budget, arithmetic; exact rationals text a string, a quoted word in a production, str , the _latex functions truth value true , false , random NAME = boolean , comparisons, and or not formula, polynomial, equation the formula_ , polynomial_ and equation functions proposition the bool_ functions matrix, set, vector, point, complex number their functions text with answer blanks blank , blank_wide , and ++ with one answer wrappers exactly , plain , vector_norm_answer and its like A truth value and a proposition are different things: p and q is true or false now, and bool_and(bool_var("p"), bool_var("q")) is a formula that can be shown, compared and evaluated. What the checker infers ¶ For every expression the checker finds the set of types it can have: A literal, a random, a budget and a generator leaf have one type. A quoted word read as $n.value is text; a generator read as $n.value is a number. A function gives the type its entry in the builtins says. cond(T, A, B) gives whatever A or B can be. An operator or a function has a type only when each operand can have a type it takes. An expression that can never be evaluated has no type, and nothing built on it is an error: the mistake is reported where it is, and not again where its result is used. A synthesized attribute has every type that some production of its nonterminal can give it. It is kept by nonterminal: value on E and value on Q are two attributes and may have two types. A module's attributes and values keep the types found when the module was checked; $n.NAME on alias.F and alias.NAME read them. The sets are found by reading the productions until none grows, so a recursive production and the order of the declarations make no difference. What is an error ¶ A use is an error when no type its operand can have is allowed: let label = "n = " ++ n let broken = label + 1 quiz.rhm:5:14: error: '+' takes a number on its left, but 'label' is text The rules are the ones the engine applies when it evaluates. For an answer and an {answer ...} hole the engine left the rule to the WeBWorK writer, which stopped on an equation; the checker now applies it. Use Takes + - * / % ^ , unary - , < <= > >= numbers and , or , not , a when guard, a require truth values = , != two values of one type: numbers, text, truth values, formulas, polynomials, equations, propositions, matrices, sets, vectors, points or complex numbers ++ text, numbers and text with blanks a function argument what its entry says; where text is wanted a number is written out, and nothing else is converted a budget update, a generator's argument, a module's starting value a number {S.NAME} and {NAME} in a prompt text, a number, or text with blanks answer , {answer ...} , blank anything but an equation or text that holds a blank $n on its own only infix and prefix take a child; everywhere else write $n.NAME a child given to infix or prefix its own copy of the attribute being computed must be text or a number a use read under a mistake what it takes, with the mistaken values in place: see below pg_context , pg_variables ; pg_width text, or a number, which is written out; a number A use that some type allows is not an error. If value is a number in one production and a formula in another, formula_negate($1.value) is accepted, and the engine refuses it in the questions where it meets a number. An expression is checked wherever it is written, also where it would never be evaluated: the unchosen branch of cond , the right side of and and or , a production that no question reaches. A file with a wrong type in such a place could generate before types were checked, and is refused. A mistake line may give a value of any kind: one root where the set of roots is the answer, the words "no solution" where a number is. The checker reads the file once more for each mistake , as the engine evaluates a finished tree under it: the lines for that mistake give their names new values, requirements are not read, and an attribute has, under the mistake, every type some production then gives it. A use that can take none of those types is an error, because generation would stop there every time the mistake was tried: value = $1 . value mistake as_text value = "two" twice = value * 2 quiz.rhm:9:11: error: under the mistake 'as_text', '*' takes a number on its left, but 'value' is text This reading teaches the checker nothing about the right working: an attribute's own type comes from its equations alone. Types are checked last, on a file that has passed every other check, so that a name that does not exist is reported once and not again for the type it does not have; type errors therefore appear only when the others are gone. rhema check does it, and so does every command that reads a file. There is one message for each wrong use: an operator with two wrong sides gives two. A message points at the operand when the operand is a name, a child or a function call. A literal or an expression in brackets has no position of its own, and the message then points at the function call around it, or at the start of its equation. What is left to the engine ¶ Whatever depends on the value and not on its type. A file that passes rhema check can still stop while generating on: a number that must be whole and is not ( factorial(1 / 2) , a budget update, an index); a division by zero, in numbers or in formulas; matrices and vectors of sizes that do not fit, a singular matrix to invert; a function outside its domain: exact_sin(1, 5) , a base above 16, a variable named 2 ; an equation with no exact solutions where one is asked for; a use that only some of an expression's types allow, as above; a number too large to be kept exact: numbers are fractions of 63-bit integers, and a sum or product that does not fit stops the question, as a division by zero does, where it would otherwise be a wrong number; a requirement that cannot be met, or a budget no production can spend. Each of these stops generation with a message of one line, and the command ends with status 1. Mistakes ¶ mistake NAME STRING declares a mistake students make. STRING says what the student does and must not be empty. Mistake names are a namespace of their own: a mistake may have the name of an attribute. A production says where the mistake is made, with a mistake line in its body: F -> "sin" F when cost >= 3 { cost = - 2 f = formula_sin ( $2 . f ) d = formula_multiply ( formula_cos ( $2 . f ), $2 . d ) mistake no_chain d = formula_cos ( $2 . f ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } The name after the mistake's must be a synthesized attribute or a local name that the production has computed above the line. The expression may use everything an equation at that place may use, the right value of its own name included. A production has at most one line for the same mistake and name. Every declared mistake must have a line in some production. A mistake line takes no part in generation. After a question is built, each mistake that some production of its tree has a line for is tried: The tree is evaluated again from the leaves up. Each node keeps its production and its children; its equations and local names are computed in order, and a line for the mistake gives its name the new value, for the lines below it and for the node. Requirements are not checked. Subtrees of imported modules are left as they are. A value is mistaken when a line for the mistake gave it a value other than the one it had, or when the expression that computed it read a mistaken value. A line that gives the same value changes nothing. The answers are read again. If none was read from a mistaken value, the mistake does not concern this question. If one was and some answer is now different, the mistake is reported with the answers it leads to. If one was and every answer is the same, wrong working would be marked right: the question is discarded and generated afresh, as after a failed requirement. Two answers are the same when a marker would take one for the other: formulas are compared as functions, at fixed points, and other values by their own equality. A mistake that ends in an arithmetic failure, such as a division by zero, is reported as leading to no answer, and the question is kept. A mistake line that cannot be evaluated for another reason, such as a value of the wrong type, stops generation with a message naming the mistake. rhema run lists, under each answer, mistake NAME: ANSWERS for every mistake reported. The PG and LaTeX output of a question does not depend on the file's mistakes. An include d file's mistakes and lines become the including file's. An import ed module's are its own: they apply to the module's questions. Precedence and rendering ¶ precedence LEVEL left | right | nonassoc OPERATOR ... gives operators a binding strength (higher binds tighter) and an associativity. A production that has an operator among its symbols takes that operator's level. The builtins infix($1, "+", $3) and prefix("\neg", $2) write their operands, adding brackets exactly where the levels and associativity require them. The operator's text need not be the symbol: E -> E * E may be written with "\cdot" . Prompt, answer, context, width ¶ prompt STRING answer EXPR context STRING width INTEGER The prompt is PGML with these replacements: Written Becomes {S.NAME} an attribute of the start symbol S {NAME} a random or let {alias.NAME} a random or let of an imported module {answer S.NAME} , {answer NAME} an answer blank graded against that value {{ , }} literal braces answer EXPR adds one blank after the prompt; it may use S.NAME and module values. A question has either answer or {answer ...} blanks, not both. context names the WeBWorK context (default Numeric ); width sets the width of every blank. Blanks in text ¶ A blank may also be part of the text a production builds: text = "Centre: " ++ blank ( point2 ( h , k )) ++ " Radius: " ++ blank_wide ( r , 4 ) blank(VALUE) is an answer blank graded against VALUE , and blank_wide(VALUE, COLUMNS) the same with a width of its own. Joined to text with ++ it makes text with blanks ; when {S.NAME} or {NAME} in the prompt holds such a value, its text and blanks go into the question in the order written. Each production then says where its own blanks are, so forms with different numbers of blanks can share a grammar. A file whose rules or lets call blank needs no answer line. A question made with no blank at all is refused when it is generated. A question with an answer line and blanks in its text is refused: its blanks come from one place. Text with blanks can only be joined with ++ and shown through the prompt; str , a comparison or a *_latex function refuses it. A blank cannot be inside mathematics, between [` and `] . Answers that carry their context ¶ Some answers are written to WeBWorK with a context of their own, so the question may be in any context and the grammar sets none: a point ( point2 , point3 ); a formula in variables other than x : the context declares the variables of every formula answer of the question and those named by pg_variables , so its blanks accept the same names; a proposition ( bool_* ): the context is a copy of WeBWorK's Boolean context, which knows p and q alone, that declares the variables of every proposition answer of the question and those named by pg_variables . The compiled file loads contextBoolean.pl for it; plain(VALUE) , a number or formula that must be worked out: the trigonometric, hyperbolic, logarithm and exponential functions are switched off ( sqrt and abs stay), so sin(pi/3) is not accepted as the value of sin(π/3). WeBWorK compares numbers with a relative tolerance of one part in a thousand. Up to 1000 that still tells a whole number from its neighbours; above it, it does not: for the answer 5040 it accepts 5041, and for 10100 it accepts 10110. A whole-number answer of 1000 or more (or -1000 or less) is therefore written with an absolute tolerance of half a unit, so that no other whole number passes; smaller ones are written as bare numbers. A fraction is the same in its numerator: from 1001 on, WeBWorK accepts (p + 1)/q for p/q , whatever q is. A fraction answer whose numerator is 1000 or more (or -1000 or less) is written with an absolute tolerance of half a step of its denominator, 1/(2q) , so that neither neighbour passes; a decimal typed in its place must then be right to within that. Smaller fractions are written as before. exactly(N) asks for the exact comparison whatever the size of N ; base_conversion.rhm uses it where the digits are the answer. Questions ¶ question NAME { start SYMBOL prompt STRING [ answer EXPR ] [ context STRING ] [ width INTEGER ] [ ATTRIBUTE = INTEGER ] ... } declares a named question over the file's productions. The top-level start , prompt , answer , context and width form the question main . A block without context or width takes the file's. ATTRIBUTE = INTEGER starts an inherited attribute at that value for this question. A file of blocks only has no main ; its first block is its default question. main cannot be used as a block's name. include and import ¶ include "FILE.rhm" import "FILE.rhm" as ALIAS include merges the other file's declarations into this one before checking. Productions, attributes, randoms, lets and precedences add up; identical declarations in both files are kept once. Of the declarations a file makes once ( start , prompt , answer , context , width ), the including file's own win. Among inherited attributes, the including file's declaration wins, then the first included one. import loads the other file as a separate module, checked on its own. Its nonterminals, randoms, lets and questions are reached as ALIAS.NAME ; its synthesized attributes are read through $n as usual; its precedences and productions are not visible. A module is loaded once per run however many files import it, and its randoms are drawn once per question. A module's own imports are private to it. A module subtree is atomic to the importer's infix : no brackets are added around it. Both look for the file beside the file that names it, then in -I directories, RHEMA_PATH and the installed library. A file that includes or imports itself, directly or through others, is refused. Sets ¶ set NAME { part "HEADING" COUNT of QUESTION ( DRAW , ...) COUNT of any ( QUESTION ( DRAW , ...), ...) distinct balanced ordered } QUESTION is main , a question of this file, or ALIAS.NAME . Each DRAW starts one inherited attribute of that question: Draw Meaning cost = 6 every question starts at 6 cost in {8, 10, 12} values taken in turn, each once before any repeats cost ~ 6 [spread 2] [low 2] [allowed {4, 6}] drawn around the mean and adjusted so the entry's mean is exactly 6 (or as close as allowed permits); spread defaults to 2, low to 0 part lines group the entries that follow under one number. distinct refuses a question of the same type and tree shape as an earlier one; balanced refuses a third equal coded answer in a row; ordered sorts each part by total budget. How a question is generated ¶ The paper's variant is derived from the assignment's name, and from the student's when one is given; it fixes every random choice below. The randoms of the file and of every module it imports are drawn; then the lets are computed in order. From the start symbol, with the inherited attributes at their starting values, each node is built: the productions for the symbol whose guards hold, and whose updates leave every budget non-negative, are the candidates; if there are none, generation stops with no rule for 'E' fits {...} ; one candidate is chosen in proportion to its weight; its updates are applied and the inherited attributes distributed to the children, which are built in turn; its equations and requirements are evaluated in order. A failed requirement builds the node again, with fresh choices, up to 40 times; after that the failure passes to the node above, which tries again in the same way. A question that still fails is started afresh, up to 200 times, before generation gives up and names the requirement that failed most often. The prompt, blanks and context are read from the finished tree. Each mistake with a line in the tree is tried. A question in which one changes the working and leaves every answer right is started afresh, within the same 200 attempts. When a failure could not have gone differently, because no random choice was involved, it is reported at once instead of retried. What the checker guarantees ¶ rhema check accepts a file only if: it parses, and every name it uses is declared: symbols, attributes, randoms, lets, builtins, aliases, questions, modules' names; every production computes every synthesized attribute its symbol carries, and an update is never a positive constant; guards and updates use only what exists before the children are built; equations and requirements use children only within range and only attributes those children carry; every builtin and generator is called with the right number of arguments, and random draws have literal arguments; no operator, function, guard, requirement, budget update, prompt, answer or mistake line is given a value that cannot have a type it takes ( Types ); every nonterminal can finish (some production for it uses only symbols that can finish), and every cycle of productions spends an inherited attribute, so no derivation can go round for ever without spending; prompts, answers, questions and sets refer to things that exist, with the right kinds of blank; every mistake is declared once, with a description, and is made in some production; every mistake line names a declared mistake and a value its production has already computed; no file includes or imports itself. What the checker cannot know is left to generation, and reported clearly when it happens: a budget no production can spend, a requirement that cannot be met, a value whose type suits in some questions and not in others, a number that must be whole, a division by zero, a mistake that always changes the working and never an answer. docs.title: The language

docs.text: A Rhema file is a sequence of declarations , in any order, encoded as UTF-8 and named with the extension .rhm . A file does one or more of three things: declares questions : a start symbol, a prompt and an answer, at the top level (the question main ) or in question blocks; declares sets : whole assignments built from questions; provides productions and attributes for other files to include or import . A file with neither questions nor sets is a library : it can be checked, included and imported, but not run. polynomial_core.rhm and matrix_core.rhm in the standard library are libraries.
docs.title: Files

docs.text: Comments run from # to the end of the line. Identifiers are a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores. By convention nonterminals start with a capital letter ( E , Q ) and attributes, randoms and lets do not; the language does not require it. Integers are decimal digits. A minus sign is an operator, except where a declaration takes a signed integer: the value in attribute , starting values in question blocks, and the draws of a set . Strings are written in double quotes and may span lines; the line breaks are part of the string. The only escapes are \" (a quote) and \\ (a backslash). Any other backslash is kept, so LaTeX is written directly: "\cdot" and "\\cdot" are the same string. Keywords are reserved: answer as attribute boolean context copy import include left let mistake nonassoc on precedence prompt question random require right set split start synth weight when width and or not true false A reserved word cannot be used as a name, also not for a local name in a production: let width = ... is a syntax error. Inside a set block, the words part , of , any , in , spread , low , allowed , distinct , balanced and ordered have a meaning, but they are not reserved and may be used as names elsewhere.
docs.title: Lexical structure

docs.text: attribute NAME = INTEGER [ copy | split ] declares an attribute whose value travels down the tree. INTEGER is its value at the root of a question, and must not be negative. The distribution says how a node passes it to its children: copy (the default) every child that is a symbol of the grammar receives the node's value; split the node's value is divided between those children, every division into non-negative whole numbers being equally likely. Leaves (generators and quoted words) receive nothing. A child that is a module symbol ( alias.F ) counts as a symbol of the grammar. The starting value can be changed from outside, with --set NAME=VALUE on the command line, an INTEGER in a question block, or a draw in a set .
docs.title: Inherited attributes

docs.text: synth NAME synth NAME on SYMBOL declares an attribute whose value travels up the tree, computed at a node from its children. on SYMBOL restricts it to one nonterminal; without it, every nonterminal must compute it. The same name may be declared on several symbols, but not both with and without on . Every production for a symbol must compute every synthesized attribute that symbol carries. A generator leaf carries one attribute, value , the number it drew; a quoted word carries value , its text. Three names are reserved for the start symbol: pg_context , the WeBWorK context of each question, pg_width , the width of its answer blanks, and pg_variables , the variables of its formula and proposition answers. When the start symbol computes the first two, they override the file's context and width for that question. pg_variables is text naming variables, such as "x y" . A formula answer is written with a context that declares the variables it holds; with pg_variables every formula answer of the question is declared in all the named ones, so a derivative that comes to 6y is entered in a blank that knows x too. A proposition answer is declared in them in the same way, as propositional variables. It may also be a let of the file, for all its questions.
docs.title: Synthesized attributes

docs.text: LHS -> SYMBOL ... [ when EXPR ] [ weight INTEGER ] { EQUATION ... } A production says that the nonterminal LHS may be made of the symbols on the right. The braces are required, even when empty. Each symbol on the right is one of: Written Meaning E a nonterminal, if the file has productions for it; otherwise a terminal that stands for its name + - * / % ^ a terminal that stands for the operator "text" a terminal that stands for the text integer_between(1, 9) a generator: a leaf that draws a number (see builtins ) calc.F or calc.F(cost = cost - 1) a nonterminal of an imported module, with starting values for its inherited attributes $1 , $2 , ... refer to these symbols, counting from 1. when EXPR is the production's guard . The production may be chosen only when it is true. It is evaluated before the children exist, so it may use inherited attributes and question-level values, but not $n . weight INTEGER (a positive integer, 1 by default) is the production's relative chance of being chosen among those whose guards hold.
docs.title: Productions

docs.text: The body holds equations and requirements, separated by line breaks or commas: NAME = EXPR , where NAME is inherited An update , applied before the children are built: the value is added to the attribute. It must not make the budget negative, and a positive constant is refused, because an update spends a budget. cost = -2 spends 2. NAME = EXPR , where NAME is synthesized Computes the attribute, after the children are built. An equation may use an attribute computed earlier in the same body by its bare name. require EXPR A condition checked after the children are built and the equations above it are computed. When it is false, the node is built again. let NAME = EXPR A local name : a value computed after the children are built, for the lines below it in the same body. The node does not carry it, so it needs no synth declaration and no other production sees it. The name must be new: an attribute, a random, a file-level let or an earlier local name of the same production is refused. Guards, updates and generator arguments are evaluated before the children exist and cannot use it. mistake NAME ATTRIBUTE = EXPR A mistake line : what a student who makes the mistake NAME computes for ATTRIBUTE here. It is skipped when the question is generated. Updates are applied in the order written; equations, local names and requirements are evaluated in the order written. B -> integer_between ( - 3 , 2 ) integer_between ( 1 , 4 ) { let upper = $1 . value + $2 . value require upper != 0 latex = "\int_ {" ++ str($1.value) ++ "} ^ {" ++ str(upper) ++ "} " value = upper }

docs.text: Form Meaning 12 , "text" a number, a string true , false the two truth values NAME an inherited attribute of the node, a random or let, or an attribute or local name computed earlier in the same production $2.NAME an attribute of the second child $2 the second child itself; only as an argument of infix and prefix S.NAME an attribute of the start symbol S ; only in prompt and answer alias.NAME a random or let of an imported module f(e, ...) a builtin function -e , not e negation e + e , - , * , / , % , ^ arithmetic on numbers e ++ e joining text, or text and answer blanks e = e , != , < , <= , > , >= comparison e and e , e or e logic Numbers are exact rationals: 1 / 3 is one third, not 0.333. = and != on text compare the strings, and on truth values they are the biconditional and exclusive or; < , <= , > and >= order numbers only. Operators bind, from loosest to tightest: or ; and ; not ; the comparisons (which do not chain); ++ (right-associative); + - ; * / % ; ^ (right-associative); unary - . Brackets group. Every value has a type, and rhema check finds the uses no type allows before anything is generated; see Types .

docs.text: random NAME = boolean random NAME = GENERATOR ( INTEGER , ...) let NAME = EXPR A random is drawn once per question, before the tree is built, and has the same value wherever it is used. Its arguments must be integer literals. A let is computed once per question, after the randoms, from randoms and earlier lets. It may call any builtin function but may not refer to the tree.

docs.text: Every value has one of these types. Nothing in a file declares a type: the checker works them out. Type Made by number a literal, a generator, a budget, arithmetic; exact rationals text a string, a quoted word in a production, str , the _latex functions truth value true , false , random NAME = boolean , comparisons, and or not formula, polynomial, equation the formula_ , polynomial_ and equation functions proposition the bool_ functions matrix, set, vector, point, complex number their functions text with answer blanks blank , blank_wide , and ++ with one answer wrappers exactly , plain , vector_norm_answer and its like A truth value and a proposition are different things: p and q is true or false now, and bool_and(bool_var("p"), bool_var("q")) is a formula that can be shown, compared and evaluated.

docs.text: For every expression the checker finds the set of types it can have: A literal, a random, a budget and a generator leaf have one type. A quoted word read as $n.value is text; a generator read as $n.value is a number. A function gives the type its entry in the builtins says. cond(T, A, B) gives whatever A or B can be. An operator or a function has a type only when each operand can have a type it takes. An expression that can never be evaluated has no type, and nothing built on it is an error: the mistake is reported where it is, and not again where its result is used. A synthesized attribute has every type that some production of its nonterminal can give it. It is kept by nonterminal: value on E and value on Q are two attributes and may have two types. A module's attributes and values keep the types found when the module was checked; $n.NAME on alias.F and alias.NAME read them. The sets are found by reading the productions until none grows, so a recursive production and the order of the declarations make no difference.

A mistake line may give a value of any kind: one root where the set of roots is the answer, the words "no solution" where a number is. The checker reads the file once more for each mistake , as the engine evaluates a finished tree under it: the lines for that mistake give their names new values, requirements are not read, and an attribute has, under the mistake, every type some production then gives it. docs.text: precedence LEVEL left | right | nonassoc OPERATOR ... gives operators a binding strength (higher binds tighter) and an associativity. A production that has an operator among its symbols takes that operator's level. The builtins infix($1, "+", $3) and prefix("\neg", $2) write their operands, adding brackets exactly where the levels and associativity require them. The operator's text need not be the symbol: E -> E * E may be written with "\cdot" .

docs.text: prompt STRING answer EXPR context STRING width INTEGER The prompt is PGML with these replacements: Written Becomes {S.NAME} an attribute of the start symbol S {NAME} a random or let {alias.NAME} a random or let of an imported module {answer S.NAME} , {answer NAME} an answer blank graded against that value {{ , }} literal braces answer EXPR adds one blank after the prompt; it may use S.NAME and module values. A question has either answer or {answer ...} blanks, not both. context names the WeBWorK context (default Numeric ); width sets the width of every blank.
docs.title: Prompt, answer, context, width

docs.text: A blank may also be part of the text a production builds: text = "Centre: " ++ blank ( point2 ( h , k )) ++ " Radius: " ++ blank_wide ( r , 4 ) blank(VALUE) is an answer blank graded against VALUE , and blank_wide(VALUE, COLUMNS) the same with a width of its own. Joined to text with ++ it makes text with blanks ; when {S.NAME} or {NAME} in the prompt holds such a value, its text and blanks go into the question in the order written. Each production then says where its own blanks are, so forms with different numbers of blanks can share a grammar. A file whose rules or lets call blank needs no answer line. A question made with no blank at all is refused when it is generated. A question with an answer line and blanks in its text is refused: its blanks come from one place. Text with blanks can only be joined with ++ and shown through the prompt; str , a comparison or a *_latex function refuses it. A blank cannot be inside mathematics, between [` and `] .
docs.title: Blanks in text

docs.text: Some answers are written to WeBWorK with a context of their own, so the question may be in any context and the grammar sets none: a point ( point2 , point3 ); a formula in variables other than x : the context declares the variables of every formula answer of the question and those named by pg_variables , so its blanks accept the same names; a proposition ( bool_* ): the context is a copy of WeBWorK's Boolean context, which knows p and q alone, that declares the variables of every proposition answer of the question and those named by pg_variables . The compiled file loads contextBoolean.pl for it; plain(VALUE) , a number or formula that must be worked out: the trigonometric, hyperbolic, logarithm and exponential functions are switched off ( sqrt and abs stay), so sin(pi/3) is not accepted as the value of sin(π/3). WeBWorK compares numbers with a relative tolerance of one part in a thousand. Up to 1000 that still tells a whole number from its neighbours; above it, it does not: for the answer 5040 it accepts 5041, and for 10100 it accepts 10110. A whole-number answer of 1000 or more (or -1000 or less) is therefore written with an absolute tolerance of half a unit, so that no other whole number passes; smaller ones are written as bare numbers. A fraction is the same in its numerator: from 1001 on, WeBWorK accepts (p + 1)/q for p/q , whatever q is. A fraction answer whose numerator is 1000 or more (or -1000 or less) is written with an absolute tolerance of half a step of its denominator, 1/(2q) , so that neither neighbour passes; a decimal typed in its place must then be right to within that. Smaller fractions are written as before. exactly(N) asks for the exact comparison whatever the size of N ; base_conversion.rhm uses it where the digits are the answer.
docs.title: Answers that carry their context

docs.text: question NAME { start SYMBOL prompt STRING [ answer EXPR ] [ context STRING ] [ width INTEGER ] [ ATTRIBUTE = INTEGER ] ... } declares a named question over the file's productions. The top-level start , prompt , answer , context and width form the question main . A block without context or width takes the file's. ATTRIBUTE = INTEGER starts an inherited attribute at that value for this question. A file of blocks only has no main ; its first block is its default question. main cannot be used as a block's name.
docs.title: Questions

docs.text: include "FILE.rhm" import "FILE.rhm" as ALIAS include merges the other file's declarations into this one before checking. Productions, attributes, randoms, lets and precedences add up; identical declarations in both files are kept once. Of the declarations a file makes once ( start , prompt , answer , context , width ), the including file's own win. Among inherited attributes, the including file's declaration wins, then the first included one. import loads the other file as a separate module, checked on its own. Its nonterminals, randoms, lets and questions are reached as ALIAS.NAME ; its synthesized attributes are read through $n as usual; its precedences and productions are not visible. A module is loaded once per run however many files import it, and its randoms are drawn once per question. A module's own imports are private to it. A module subtree is atomic to the importer's infix : no brackets are added around it. Both look for the file beside the file that names it, then in -I directories, RHEMA_PATH and the installed library. A file that includes or imports itself, directly or through others, is refused.
docs.title: include and import

docs.text: set NAME { part "HEADING" COUNT of QUESTION ( DRAW , ...) COUNT of any ( QUESTION ( DRAW , ...), ...) distinct balanced ordered } QUESTION is main , a question of this file, or ALIAS.NAME . Each DRAW starts one inherited attribute of that question: Draw Meaning cost = 6 every question starts at 6 cost in {8, 10, 12} values taken in turn, each once before any repeats cost ~ 6 [spread 2] [low 2] [allowed {4, 6}] drawn around the mean and adjusted so the entry's mean is exactly 6 (or as close as allowed permits); spread defaults to 2, low to 0 part lines group the entries that follow under one number. distinct refuses a question of the same type and tree shape as an earlier one; balanced refuses a third equal coded answer in a row; ordered sorts each part by total budget.
docs.title: Sets

docs.text: The paper's variant is derived from the assignment's name, and from the student's when one is given; it fixes every random choice below. The randoms of the file and of every module it imports are drawn; then the lets are computed in order. From the start symbol, with the inherited attributes at their starting values, each node is built: the productions for the symbol whose guards hold, and whose updates leave every budget non-negative, are the candidates; if there are none, generation stops with no rule for 'E' fits {...} ; one candidate is chosen in proportion to its weight; its updates are applied and the inherited attributes distributed to the children, which are built in turn; its equations and requirements are evaluated in order. A failed requirement builds the node again, with fresh choices, up to 40 times; after that the failure passes to the node above, which tries again in the same way. A question that still fails is started afresh, up to 200 times, before generation gives up and names the requirement that failed most often. The prompt, blanks and context are read from the finished tree. Each mistake with a line in the tree is tried. A question in which one changes the working and leaves every answer right is started afresh, within the same 200 attempts. When a failure could not have gone differently, because no random choice was involved, it is reported at once instead of retried.
docs.title: How a question is generated

docs.text: rhema check accepts a file only if: it parses, and every name it uses is declared: symbols, attributes, randoms, lets, builtins, aliases, questions, modules' names; every production computes every synthesized attribute its symbol carries, and an update is never a positive constant; guards and updates use only what exists before the children are built; equations and requirements use children only within range and only attributes those children carry; every builtin and generator is called with the right number of arguments, and random draws have literal arguments; no operator, function, guard, requirement, budget update, prompt, answer or mistake line is given a value that cannot have a type it takes ( Types ); every nonterminal can finish (some production for it uses only symbols that can finish), and every cycle of productions spends an inherited attribute, so no derivation can go round for ever without spending; prompts, answers, questions and sets refer to things that exist, with the right kinds of blank; every mistake is declared once, with a description, and is made in some production; every mistake line names a declared mistake and a value its production has already computed; no file includes or imports itself. What the checker cannot know is left to generation, and reported clearly when it happens: a budget no production can spend, a requirement that cannot be met, a value whose type suits in some questions and not in others, a number that must be whole, a division by zero, a mistake that always changes the working and never an answer.

docs.text: Difficulty is a budget ¶ The questions of chapter 1 are all equally hard. This file asks sums, differences and products of any length, and how long they are is decided when the questions are generated. # Sums, differences and products whose difficulty is a budget. attribute cost = 4 split synth value on E synth latex on E precedence 1 left + - precedence 2 left * start E E -> E + E when cost >= 1 weight 3 { cost = - 1 value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , "+" , $3 ) } E -> E - E when cost >= 2 weight 2 { cost = - 2 require $1 . value != $3 . value value = $1 . value - $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , "-" , $3 ) } E -> E * E when cost >= 3 weight 2 { cost = - 3 value = $1 . value * $3 . value latex = infix ( $1 , " \\ cdot" , $3 ) } E -> integer_between ( 2 , 9 ) when cost = 0 { value = $1 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) } prompt "What is the value of [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=2 --count 3 1. What is the value of [`4 + (4 + 6)`]? answer: 14 2. What is the value of [`3 - 4`]? answer: -1 3. What is the value of [`8 + 2 + 3`]? answer: 13 $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=8 --count 3 1. What is the value of [`(4 - 6 + (3 + 4)) \cdot (5 + 8)`]? answer: 65 2. What is the value of [`3 + (7 + 7 + (5 + 7) + (4 - 2 + 5))`]? answer: 36 3. What is the value of [`(6 + 2 - (8 + 5)) \cdot (7 + 8)`]? answer: -75 Productions that refer to themselves ¶ E -> E + E says that an E may be two smaller E s with a plus between them. A grammar like this can make expressions of any size; on its own it would never stop. Something has to say how far to go. Inherited attributes ¶ That something is an inherited attribute , declared with attribute : attribute cost = 4 split Synthesized attributes, from chapter 1, travel up the tree: a node computes them from its children. Inherited attributes travel down: a node receives one from its parent before its children exist. cost starts at 4 at the root (or at whatever --set cost=N says) and is handed down. split says how it is handed down. At each production, what is left of the budget is divided between the children that are symbols of the grammar, in every possible way with equal chance. The other choice, copy , gives every child the whole value; it suits settings that are not spent, such as a limit on the number of digits. Spending ¶ Each production says what it costs: E -> E + E when cost >= 1 weight 3 { cost = - 1 ... } cost = -1 takes one from the budget before it is divided between the two E s. So a sum costs 1, a difference 2 and a product 3, and a number costs nothing. Whatever budget the root starts with, the finished question has spent exactly that much: --set cost=2 gives one difference or two sums, never a product. when cost >= 1 is a guard : the production may only be chosen when it holds. A guard can only look at inherited attributes, because the children do not exist yet when the choice is made. The number production says when cost = 0 , so a number appears exactly where the budget has run out. Among the productions whose guards hold, one is chosen at random, in proportion to its weight (1 when not given). The weights here make sums more common than products. Every budget must be spendable ¶ When a node receives a budget that no production can take, generation stops. Remove the sum production and ask for a budget of 1, which only a sum could spend: $ rhema run gap.rhm --set cost=1 gap.rhm: error: no rule for 'E' fits {cost=1} This is not retried, because no amount of retrying could help: the grammar has no way to spend 1. A grammar that spends a budget should be able to spend every whole number from its smallest question upwards. With prices 1, 2 and 3 and a leaf at 0, this one can. The compiler also refuses a recursion that does not spend. Delete the cost = -1 line from the sum production and check the file: $ rhema check loop.rhm loop.rhm:13:1: error: this rule can reach 'E' again without spending any inherited attribute, so a derivation could circle forever; make the loop consume a budget, for example 'cost = -1' Requirements ¶ The difference production says require $1 . value != $3 . value A require is checked after the children are built. When it fails, that subtree is built again with fresh random choices. Here it rules out differences of zero, such as 7 - 7 , which would make a question cheaper than its price. Prefer guards to requirements where you can: a guard prevents a bad choice, a requirement discards one after the work is done. Brackets come from precedence ¶ precedence 1 left + - precedence 2 left * infix($1, "+", $3) writes its operands with brackets only where the precedence table needs them, which is why the questions above read 4 + (4 + 6) and (6 + 2 - (8 + 5)) \cdot (7 + 8) with no extra brackets. The operator's text may differ from its symbol: the product is the symbol * in the grammar and \cdot in the question. Choosing a difficulty ¶ The budget is how a teacher asks for an easier or a harder question of the same kind: $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=3 $ rhema run budget.rhm --set cost=12 Every grammar in the library spends a budget called cost in this way, with prices chosen for its subject; the difficulty page lists them. Chapter 7 shows how a whole assignment fixes the average budget of its questions rather than each one. Next: chapter 3 looks at what the attributes can hold besides numbers and text.

docs.text: A first question ¶ Here is a complete Rhema file. Save it as first.rhm . # The smallest useful question: the sum of two numbers. synth value on E synth latex on E start E E -> integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) "+" integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) { value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) ++ " + " ++ str ( $3 . value ) } prompt "What is [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value Check it, then ask for three questions: $ rhema check first.rhm first.rhm: OK (1 rules; questions: main; sets: none) $ rhema run first.rhm --count 3 1. What is [`82 + 40`]? answer: 122 2. What is [`83 + 52`]? answer: 135 3. What is [`36 + 76`]? answer: 112 Productions ¶ A Rhema file is a grammar. Its rules, called productions , say what a symbol may be made of. This file has one: E -> integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) "+" integer_between ( 10 , 99 ) { ... } Read it as: an E is a number from 10 to 99, a plus sign, and another such number. start E says that a question is an E . To make a question, the compiler starts from E , picks a production for it, and builds whatever the production asks for, which is how a question becomes a tree: E ├── integer_between(10, 99) 82 ├── "+" └── integer_between(10, 99) 40 integer_between(10, 99) is a generator : a leaf that draws a value. A quoted string such as "+" is a leaf that stands for itself. Attributes ¶ A tree on its own is not a question. The braces after a production say what to compute at that node, from its children: value = $1 . value + $3 . value latex = str ( $1 . value ) ++ " + " ++ str ( $3 . value ) $1 is the first symbol on the right of the arrow, $3 the third. Every generator leaf carries its drawn number as value ; str turns a number into text and ++ joins text. So at the E above, value is 122 and latex is 82 + 40 . These are synthesized attributes : computed from the children, on the way back up the tree. Each has to be declared, with the symbol that carries it: synth value on E synth latex on E The compiler checks that every production for E says how to compute both. Leave one out and it will not compile: $ rhema check first.rhm first.rhm:8:1: error: rule 'E' does not say how to compute 'latex'; add 'latex = ...' inside its braces The prompt and the answer ¶ The last two lines turn the finished tree into a question: prompt "What is [` {E.latex} `]?" answer E . value {E.latex} in the prompt is replaced by the latex attribute of the start symbol. The prompt is written in WeBWorK's PGML, so [`...`] marks mathematics. answer names the attribute the student's answer is graded against. This is the point of writing questions this way. The text the student reads and the answer the grader expects are two attributes of one tree, computed from the same drawn numbers, so they cannot drift apart. There is no answer key to keep in step with the questions. What the compiler checks ¶ Before any question is generated, rhema check makes sure that every symbol used has productions or is a leaf, every synthesized attribute is computed by every production that must carry it, the prompt and answer name attributes that exist, every builtin function is called with the right number of arguments, no operator or function is given a value that cannot have a type it takes (text added to a number, a number where a formula is wanted). These are checked once, for the file, not for each question drawn. A file that checks will not fail half way through a paper for one of these reasons. Next: the questions above are all equally hard. Chapter 2 gives a grammar a budget, so that one file can ask easy and hard questions of the same kind.

docs.text: Building on the library ¶ Rhema comes with grammars for most of first-year mathematics. A file can use their parts without copying them. This one asks for second derivatives, using the expressions of the library's calculus grammar. # Second derivatives, built on the library's expressions. import "calculus.rhm" as calc attribute cost = 4 copy synth text on M synth answer_value on M start M M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) { answer_value = differentiate ( differentiate ( $1 . formula , "x" ), "x" ) require not formula_is_zero ( answer_value ) text = "Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = " ++ $1 . latex ++ "`]." } prompt " {M.text} " answer M . answer_value $ rhema run import.rhm --count 3 1. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = x^{3} - (\ln\left(x\right) - x)`]. answer: Formula(3*2*x--1/x^2) 2. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = x \cdot \sin\left(x\right)`]. answer: Formula(cos(x)+cos(x)-x*sin(x)) 3. Find the second derivative of [`f(x) = 5 - x - e^{3 \cdot x}`]. answer: Formula(-(exp(3*x)*3*3)) import ¶ import "calculus.rhm" as calc import loads another file as a module : it is checked on its own, and everything it declares is reached through the name after as . In calculus.rhm From this file the nonterminal F calc.F , on the right of a production its randoms and lets calc.NAME in an expression, {calc.NAME} in a prompt its questions calc.derivative , in a set (chapter 7) Nothing in the module can clash with this file. The library's two Boolean grammars both have a start symbol Q , an attribute cost and a random phrasing , drawn differently; imported as bool and laws they sit side by side. The file is looked for beside this one, then in the installed library, so calculus.rhm needs no path. ( The rhema command lists every place searched.) Using an imported symbol ¶ M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) { answer_value = differentiate ( differentiate ( $1 . formula , "x" ), "x" ) ... } calc.F is expanded with the module's own productions. $1 is that subtree, and its synthesized attributes are read as usual: $1.formula and $1.latex are what calculus.rhm computes at F . The checker knows $1 is a calc.F and checks the names against the module. Write $1.value for $1.latex and it says: $ rhema check import_bad.rhm import_bad.rhm:15:3: error: $1 is calc.F, which does not carry 'value'; it has formula, latex, constant, monomial, constants_used, linear_terms, power Arguments at the boundary ¶ calc.F(cost = cost) sets the module's inherited attribute cost for that subtree. An attribute not named takes the module's own default; calc.F alone would start at calculus.rhm 's attribute cost = 7 . The argument is computed in this file, before the subtree exists, and the module's budget is its own: the module never sees this file's cost , only the value handed to it. That is what lets grammars priced on different scales work together. A derivative of 8 is harder than a proposition of 8, so a file that offers either writes the exchange rate where they meet: M -> calc . F ( cost = cost ) "derivative" { ... } M -> bool . E ( cost = cost + 2 ) "boolean" { ... } When this file's attribute is split , cost = cost hands the module the share a local symbol would have received, so the budget is still spent exactly across the boundary. include, for extending ¶ include "file.rhm" is the older, simpler mechanism: it pastes the other file's declarations into this one, with no prefix. Use it to extend a grammar, adding productions to its symbols or asking its question with a different prompt. Use import to combine grammars. docs.text: Installing with opam ¶ rhema is written in OCaml and published through opam , OCaml's package manager. Installing it takes three steps: install opam, let opam set itself up, and ask it for rhema . You do not need to know OCaml, and nothing here asks you to write any. The steps are for Linux and macOS, where rhema is built and tested on every change. On Windows, install WSL and follow the Linux steps inside it. If you already use opam, go straight to step 3 . 1. Install opam ¶ Use your system's package manager: System Command macOS, with Homebrew brew install opam macOS, with MacPorts sudo port install opam Debian and Ubuntu sudo apt install opam Fedora sudo dnf install opam Arch Linux sudo pacman -S opam On any other system, or to have the newest opam, use opam's own installer. It downloads one program and asks where to put it: $ bash -c "sh <(curl -fsSL https://opam.ocaml.org/install.sh)" The installer brings opam alone, not the tools opam works with: a C compiler, make , curl , unzip and, on Linux, bubblewrap . Install those first. On Debian and Ubuntu that is sudo apt install build-essential curl unzip bubblewrap ; on macOS, xcode-select --install provides the compiler and make , and the rest are already there. opam's install page covers more systems. Check that opam is there: $ opam --version 2.4.1 Any version 2 will do. If opam later warns that a newer version has security fixes, the installer above replaces the old one. 2. Set opam up ¶ Run this as yourself, without sudo : $ opam init It downloads the list of packages, asks one question, and then gives you an OCaml compiler: the system's own if there is one, otherwise one it builds, which takes a few minutes. Everything it installs goes into ~/.opam . The question is whether opam may add a line to your shell's startup file: Do you want opam to configure zsh? > 1. Yes, update ~/.zshrc 2. Yes, but don't setup any hooks. You'll have to run eval $(opam env) whenever you change your current 'opam switch' 3. Select a different shell 4. Specify another config file to update instead 5. No, I'll remember to run eval $(opam env) when I need opam [1/2/3/4/5] Choose 1 : that line is how every new terminal finds the commands opam installs. (An older opam asks the same thing as a yes-or-no question; answer y .) For the terminal you are in now, run: $ eval $(opam env) In a container opam builds packages in a sandbox, which does not work inside Docker and similar containers. There, run opam init --disable-sandboxing instead. 3. Install rhema ¶ $ opam update $ opam install rhema opam update fetches the current list of packages; straight after opam init the list is already current and the command does no harm. opam then says what it is about to install, rhema and the tools it is built with, and asks whether to go on: The following actions will be performed: === install 7 packages - install dune 3.24.2 [required by rhema] - install menhir 20260209 [required by rhema] - install menhirCST 20260209 [required by menhir] - install menhirGLR 20260209 [required by menhir] - install menhirLib 20260209 [required by menhir] - install menhirSdk 20260209 [required by menhir] - install rhema 0.2.0 Answer y . Building takes a minute or two. Then: $ rhema --version rhema 0.2.0 (the Rhema language, RHM project) Note 0.2.0 was released on 2026-11-16. Until the opam repository has accepted it, opam installs 0.1.1; opam update followed by opam upgrade rhema brings 0.2.0 once it is there. The package holds the rhema command and the library of grammars. The library is in the directory opam var rhema:share prints, and rhema looks there by itself, so an import of a library file works from any directory. That is everything the tutorial needs. Go on to A first question . Updating and removing ¶ To move to a new release of rhema when one is published: $ opam update $ opam upgrade rhema To remove it: $ opam remove rhema If something goes wrong ¶ rhema: command not found The terminal does not have opam's settings. Run eval $(opam env) . If every new terminal needs this, the line from step 2 was not added: run opam init again and choose 1 this time. opam finds no package named rhema Its list of packages is older than rhema . Run opam update and try again. opam says rhema cannot be installed with your version of OCaml rhema needs OCaml 4.14 or later, and an opam set up some years ago may hold an older compiler; ocaml -version shows which. Build a newer one beside it, then install rhema there: $ opam switch create rhema 5.5.2 $ eval $(opam env --switch=rhema) $ opam install rhema A build stops because cc , gcc or make is missing The build tools named in step 1 are not installed. Install them and run opam install rhema again. For anything else, open an issue on GitHub with the last lines opam printed.

docs.text: Mistakes students make ¶ A right answer does not always come from right working. A student who believes that a product is differentiated factor by factor gets x \cdot 0 right, and one who subtracts the smaller number from the larger gets 7 - 3 right. A grammar can say what a mistake is. rhema then shows what each mistake leads to, and never asks a question in which a mistake changes the working and the answer still comes out right. # Derivatives worked out rule by rule, and two mistakes students make. attribute cost = 5 split mistake factor_by_factor "differentiates a product factor by factor" mistake no_chain "leaves out the derivative of the inside" synth f on F # the function synth d on F # its derivative synth latex on F synth f on T synth d on T synth latex on T start F F -> F "+" F when cost >= 1 weight 2 { cost = - 1 require $1 . latex != $3 . latex f = formula_add ( $1 . f , $3 . f ) d = formula_add ( $1 . d , $3 . d ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } F -> F "\cdot" F when cost >= 3 weight 2 { cost = - 3 require $1 . latex != $3 . latex f = formula_multiply ( $1 . f , $3 . f ) d = formula_add ( formula_multiply ( $1 . d , $3 . f ), formula_multiply ( $1 . f , $3 . d )) mistake factor_by_factor d = formula_multiply ( $1 . d , $3 . d ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } F -> "sin" F when cost >= 2 { cost = - 2 f = formula_sin ( $2 . f ) d = formula_multiply ( formula_cos ( $2 . f ), $2 . d ) mistake no_chain d = formula_cos ( $2 . f ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } F -> T when cost <= 1 { f = $1 . f d = $1 . d latex = $1 . latex } T -> "x" when cost = 0 { f = formula_variable ( "x" ) d = formula_constant ( 1 ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } T -> integer_between ( 2 , 6 ) "x" when cost = 1 { cost = - 1 f = formula_multiply ( formula_constant ( $1 . value ), formula_variable ( "x" )) d = formula_constant ( $1 . value ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } prompt "Differentiate [` {F.latex} `] with respect to [`x`]." answer F . d $ rhema run mistakes.rhm --set cost=6 --count 4 1. Differentiate [`\sin\left(x \cdot 5 \cdot x\right)`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(cos(x*5*x)*(5*x+x*5)) mistake factor_by_factor: Formula(cos(x*5*x)*5) mistake no_chain: Formula(cos(x*5*x)) 2. Differentiate [`6 \cdot x \cdot x + 6 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(6*x+6*x+6) mistake factor_by_factor: Formula(12) 3. Differentiate [`4 \cdot x \cdot \sin\left(x\right)`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(4*sin(x)+4*x*cos(x)) mistake factor_by_factor: Formula(4*cos(x)) 4. Differentiate [`2 \cdot x + 3 \cdot x + x + 4 \cdot x`] with respect to [`x`]. answer: Formula(10) Under each answer is what each mistake leads to. Question 3 holds a sine and lists no no_chain : the inside of sin(x) is x , its derivative is 1, and leaving it out changes nothing. Question 4 has no product and no sine, so there is no mistake to make. Declaring a mistake ¶ mistake no_chain "leaves out the derivative of the inside" names a mistake and says, in a few words, what the student does. The text is for people: it is kept with the mistake and is what a report or a hint would show. Where the mistake is made ¶ A mistake is made at a step of the working, and a step is a production. The production for a sine computes the derivative, and then says what the mistaken student computes in its place: F -> "sin" F when cost >= 2 { cost = - 2 f = formula_sin ( $2 . f ) d = formula_multiply ( formula_cos ( $2 . f ), $2 . d ) mistake no_chain d = formula_cos ( $2 . f ) latex = formula_latex ( f ) } A mistake line , mistake NAME ATTRIBUTE = EXPRESSION , is no part of the question. When a question is generated it is skipped, and the node carries the right d . It is read only afterwards, when the finished tree is worked out again as that student would. Everything else stays right. A student who leaves out the inside derivative still adds and multiplies correctly, so in x \cdot \sin(2x) the mistaken d of the sine goes up through the product rule as it stands, and the answer comes out as sin(2x) + x \cdot cos(2x) . This is why the grammar computes the derivative production by production, as an attribute, and does not call differentiate once at the top: a mistake can only travel through working that the grammar itself spells out. What the engine does with it ¶ After a question is built and its answers are known, each mistake that some production of the tree has a line for is tried. The tree is evaluated again from the leaves up, reading that mistake's lines, and the answers are read again. A value is mistaken when a line gave it a value other than the right one, or when it was computed from a mistaken value. Then one of four things is true: No value changes. Every line gave the value the production had already computed, as in sin(x) . The mistake is not made in this question, and nothing is listed. The mistaken values never reach an answer. The mistake says nothing about this question either. A file that also asked for the function itself, answer F.f , would build the same products and sines and list no mistakes, since no d is read. An answer changes. The mistake shows, and is listed with what it leads to. A mistaken value reaches an answer and every answer is still right. Wrong working would earn full marks, so the question is thrown away and built afresh. Answers are compared as a marker compares them. Two formulas are the same answer when they are the same function, however they are written. So in every question rhema generates, a mistake that changes the working changes an answer. The last case is rare in this grammar; it is common in others. With mistake smaller_from_larger value = cond(value < 0, -value, value) on a difference, 2 - 5 - (1 - 9) is such a question: the right working gives -3 - (-8) = 5 , and the mistaken one 3 - 8 , taken as 8 - 3 = 5 . If a mistake changes the working of every question and the answer of none, generation gives up and names it: zero.rhm: error: could not generate a question after 200 attempts; the most frequent failure (200 of 200) was: the mistake 'one_more' gives the right answer What a line may say ¶ A mistake line gives another value to something the production has already computed: a synthesized attribute of its symbol, or a local name. It is evaluated where it is written and may use everything above it, the right value of its own name included: value = $1 . value - $3 . value mistake smaller_from_larger value = cond ( value < 0 , - value , value ) The lines below it then see the mistaken value. A requirement is not checked again under a mistake; requirements shape the question, and the question is already built. A mistake may lead to no value at all, such as a division by zero. The question is kept, and the listing says no answer . In the library ¶ Four of the library's grammars declare mistakes: calculus.rhm , complex.rhm , boolean.rhm and the polynomial expansions. The library page lists them. Run any of them to see what they lead to: $ rhema run calculus.rhm --question derivative Limits ¶ A mistake belongs to the file that declares it, and to files that include that file. A subtree built from an imported module's symbol is taken as it is: the importer's mistakes are not looked for inside it, and the module's own apply to the module's own questions. The mistaken answers are shown by rhema run . The WeBWorK and LaTeX output of a question is the same as without mistakes. A listed mistake says the question can tell it apart, not that the paper tests it. A paper of questions like sin(x) lists no no_chain and finds no student who makes it; look at the listing to see what a paper covers.

docs.text: Prompts, contexts, blanks ¶ A question can have several parts, each with its own answer blank. This one asks two things about one sequence. # One sequence, two answer blanks. random first = integer_between ( - 10 , 10 ) random step = nonzero_integer_between ( - 6 , 6 ) random n = integer_between ( 8 , 15 ) let nth = first + ( n - 1 ) * step let sum = n * ( 2 * first + ( n - 1 ) * step ) / 2 synth kind on Q start Q Q -> "arithmetic" { kind = "arithmetic" } prompt "An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = {first} `] and common difference [`d = {step} `]. (a) Find [`a_ {{ {n} }} `]. {answer nth} (b) Find the sum of its first [` {n} `] terms. {answer sum} " $ rhema run prompts.rhm --count 1 1. An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = -2`] and common difference [`d = 1`]. (a) Find [`a_{12}`]. [___] (b) Find the sum of its first [`12`] terms. [___] answers: 9; 42 Compiled, each {answer ...} becomes a WeBWorK answer blank graded on its own: $ rhema prompts.rhm --count 1 -o - DOCUMENT(); loadMacros("PGstandard.pl", "MathObjects.pl", "PGML.pl"); Context("Numeric"); BEGIN_PGML An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = -2`] and common difference [`d = 1`]. (a) Find [`a_{12}`]. [_____]{9} (b) Find the sum of its first [`12`] terms. [_____]{42} END_PGML ENDDOCUMENT(); What a prompt may contain ¶ A prompt is a string, and a string may run over several lines; the line breaks are kept. Inside it, braces mark the places Rhema fills in: Written Becomes {E.latex} an attribute of the start symbol {first} a random or a let {answer E.value} an answer blank graded against an attribute of the start symbol {answer sum} an answer blank graded against a random or a let {{ and }} a literal { and } {calc.given} a random or let of an imported module (chapter 6) Everything else is passed to WeBWorK as written. Prompts are PGML, so [`...`] is mathematics and a blank line starts a new paragraph. The doubled braces matter in LaTeX. a_{12} needs braces around 12 , and n must be filled in between them, so the prompt says a_{{{n}}} : a literal { , then the value of n , then a literal } . docs.text: A whole assignment ¶ An assignment is more than questions drawn one at a time. It has parts, a range of difficulty, no two questions alike. A set says all of that in the file, and rhema turns it into one paper. # Week 3: sequences, differentiation and logic, as one assignment. import "questions.rhm" as seq import "calculus.rhm" as calc import "boolean.rhm" as bool set week3 { part "Sequences" 1 of seq . main part "Differentiation" 3 of calc . derivative ( cost ~ 6 spread 2 low 2 ) 1 of calc . integral ( cost in { 5 , 7 }) part "Logic" 3 of bool . main ( cost in { 8 , 10 , 12 }) distinct balanced ordered } The file has no question of its own. It imports the sequence question of chapter 5 and two library grammars, and declares a set: $ rhema run assignment.rhm --run week3 week3: 8 questions in 3 parts 1. Sequences 1 [seq.main; ] An arithmetic sequence has first term [`a_1 = 0`] and common difference [`d = 5`]. (a) Find [`a_{14}`]. [___] (b) Find the sum of its first [`14`] terms. [___] answers: 65; 455 2. Differentiation 2(a) [calc.derivative; cost 5] Differentiate the function with respect to x: [`f(x) = \tan\left(\ln\left(x\right) + x\right)`]. answer: Formula((1/x+1)/cos(ln(x)+x)^2) ... budget means: part 1 Sequences: part 2 Differentiation: cost 5.75 over 4 part 3 Logic: cost 10.00 over 3 Entries ¶ 3 of calc . derivative ( cost ~ 6 spread 2 low 2 ) An entry asks for a number of questions of one type: main or a named question of this file, or alias.name from an imported module. In brackets, it says how to start the question's budgets, in one of three ways: cost = 6 Every question of the entry starts at 6. cost in {8, 10, 12} Each question takes one of the values, and the list is used up before any value repeats: three questions get 8, 10 and 12 in some order. cost ~ 6 spread 2 Budgets are drawn around 6, with a spread of about 2, and then adjusted so that their mean is exactly 6. low 2 keeps every budget at 2 or above. allowed {4, 6, 8} restricts the draw to those values, for a grammar whose forms only exist at certain prices; the mean is then as close to 6 as they allow. The last form is how difficulty is meant to be set for an assignment: not "every derivative costs 6", which makes them all alike, but "the derivatives average 6", which gives some easier and some harder, at a known level overall. The listing ends with the mean of each part's budgets to show it. N of any(A, B) draws each of the N questions from the listed types evenly. Parts and numbering ¶ part "Heading" starts a part. Its questions are numbered 1(a) , 1(b) and so on, under the heading. A set without part lines numbers each question on its own: 1 , 2 , 3 . Constraints ¶ distinct No two questions have the same shape: the same productions, in the same places, with only the numbers different. 3 + 4 and 7 + 2 are one shape. Questions of different types are never repeats of each other. (In 0.1.1 two named questions on the same rule, such as seq.nth and seq.sum , counted as repeats; 0.2.0 has the fix.) balanced No three questions in a row with the same coded answer, for questions answered with true/false or a small code such as 0, 1, 2. ordered Within a part, easier questions first, by total budget. When a constraint cannot be met, such as distinct over more questions than a grammar has shapes, rhema says which question it could not place instead of trying for ever. The same paper every time ¶ The set's name is the assignment's name, and the paper is fixed by it: running week3 today and next month gives the same questions. Chapter 8 covers giving each student a paper of their own, and getting the paper into WeBWorK. Next: chapter 8.
